issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The profile is for a male patient with police trauma, but two trigger items and the body-shame appraisal are specifically sexual-trauma themed. That is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type unless there is an additional sexual trauma history, which is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: Within the trigger/appraisal cluster, the content centers on sexual victimization, while the rest of the profile does not describe corresponding sexual-trauma memory content or threat meaning. This makes the selected items clinically incoherent as a single trauma-linked PTSD profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Door/window checking suggests a home-intrusion or generalized safety threat, but the trigger and appraisal content centers on sexualized trauma cues. That threat item is not well linked to the rest of the selected profile and pulls the formulation in a different direction.

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a police trauma in a 47-year-old male bus driver, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is hard to reconcile unless the index event involved sexual assault or exposure to sexual violence in a highly personal way; nothing else in the profile supports that specificity.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is more characteristic of sexual assault or severe bodily violation. In this profile it does not cohere with the police trauma framing, and it is reinforced only by the sexual-trauma-specific trigger, creating an implausible subtheme not supported by the rest of the nodes.

vignette:
David is a 47-year-old North American man who has worked for years as a city bus driver, a job that once suited him for its routine and the steady, familiar rhythm of moving through the same neighborhoods each day. He is single and lives alone. When he speaks about the event that brought him into treatment, he does so haltingly, and even in the first sessions he often covers his face with both hands as if to block something out. Talking about it at all is difficult for him because the memory does not stay in the past; as soon as he begins to describe it, he feels it come sharply to mind again.

The traumatic event involved police. On the day it happened, David had been on duty and was pulled into a police encounter that left him feeling exposed, powerless, and unsafe. What stands out in the way he recounts it is not a detached sequence of facts but the force with which certain moments still hit him when they appear in his mind without warning. The sight of officers near his route, a patrol car at an intersection, or even the suggestion that he should explain what happened to someone can bring the whole thing back suddenly. He describes these moments as if the memory ambushes him. He can be in the driver's seat, focused on traffic, and then catch sight of police activity ahead and feel his mind pulled back before he has any chance to prepare himself.

In the weeks after the incident, David noticed himself changing in ways that felt sensible to him at the time. He had come to believe that the world was dangerous in a more global, permanent way than he had understood before. He was increasingly certain that people could not be trusted, and this was not limited to police. The feeling spread outward. He found himself pulling away from other people generally, declining invitations, keeping conversations short, and spending more time alone in his apartment. He also felt, in his own words, cut off from the sense of community he used to have. Driving the bus had once made him feel part of the city's daily life; over time he experienced himself as separate from it, watching people get on and off while feeling no real connection to them.

At work, his symptoms became woven into ordinary parts of the day. Police presence was especially difficult because he encountered it regularly on city streets. If he saw officers near a stop or standing beside a cruiser, he would feel his body tense and his attention narrow. On some days the effort to keep driving safely while these reactions were happening left him struggling to concentrate. He noticed he was more irritable with passengers and other drivers than he had been before. Small frustrations could set him off into angry outbursts, and he was troubled by how quickly his temper now came forward. He did not describe this as losing control without reason; from his perspective he was on guard in a world that had shown itself to be unsafe, and he felt constantly braced for something to go wrong.

Outside work, David developed habits meant to get him through the day and the night. When memories came up suddenly, he would cover his face with his hands, as if shutting out the image might shut down the surge that came with it. In his apartment he often turned on loud music or the television, using sound to drown out his thoughts. Silence felt risky. Quiet left too much room for the event to come back to mind. He also became preoccupied with checking doors and windows. He would lock them, then return to check again, and sometimes again after that, unable to settle until he had reassured himself. Even then the relief did not last long.

These changes narrowed his life over months. Avoiding people meant he had fewer conversations and less support, and his sense of mistrust deepened into a daily stance toward the world. His work environment, once familiar, now contained repeated reminders of what had happened, especially whenever police were visible along his route. He began to feel that nowhere was fully safe and no one was fully reliable. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by how often the memory came back and by the effort of managing himself around it. What finally brought him in was the recognition that his life had become organized around getting through the next trigger-keeping his head down, shutting people out, turning the volume up, checking the locks again. What frightens him most is the sense that this is now how the world is: dangerous, untrustworthy, and stripped of the connection he once felt to other people. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to drive his route, go home, and live through an ordinary day without feeling ambushed by the past.
